summaries.example: Imagine a classroom garden. Each plant, insect, and child changes and affects what happens next. Hartshorne might say that the living parts have their own small kinds of experience, while the whole garden is a collection rather than one giant feeling creature. The example also shows his idea that good leadership listens and responds instead of controlling every detail.
summaries.summary: Charles Hartshorne was a twentieth-century philosopher who wrote about God, change, value, and the natural world. He defended belief in God, but he did not describe God exactly as many traditional thinkers did. Classical theism often pictures God as completely unchanging and all-powerful. Hartshorne instead described a God who is everlasting, knows what can be known, responds to creatures, and shares in the world’s joys and suffering. He called this a neoclassical or process view. Hartshorne also defended psychicalism, the idea that every concrete, active part of nature has some tiny kind of experience. This does not mean that rocks, cells, or electrons think like people. It means that feeling or activity may be present in simpler forms throughout nature. He thought this view could connect science and human experience better than a sharp split between mind and matter. His method was to list possible answers, study what earlier philosophers had said, and seek a moderate position between extremes. He also argued that nature has value in itself, not only because it is useful to humans. His work influenced discussions of religion, environmental ethics, process philosophy, and the meaning of change.
key_ideas: Hartshorne thought that arguments for God work more like strands woven into a cable than like one single proof.
He described God as always changing and responding, while still being perfectly good and reliable.
He believed nature contains many active centers of experience, not only human minds.
He used history, careful comparisons, and a middle path between extreme views.
His ideas connect religion, science, nature, freedom, beauty, and care for the environment.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hartshorne asks large questions that still matter: What is God like? How can freedom and suffering exist? Is nature valuable even when it is not useful to people? Can science explain everything important about experience? His answers are disputed, but they encourage people to connect careful reasoning with respect for living beings and the changing world.

important_terms.definition: The study of what is most basic and real, such as time, change, mind, and God.
The view that all concrete, active parts of nature have some very small form of feeling or experience.
The belief that God exists, joined with philosophical arguments about what God is like.
The idea that reality is always becoming and changing, not simply staying fixed.
A way to judge what is good, valuable, beautiful, or worth caring about.

questions_to_think_about: Can something change and still keep an important identity?
Would a perfectly good God need to listen and respond to the world?
Can animals, plants, or tiny living parts have any kind of experience?
Is finding a middle way always wiser than choosing one extreme?

summaries.example: Suppose a friend tells you about a painful event. If you genuinely know what happened, that knowledge changes you: you now have a different understanding and a different relationship to your friend. Hartshorne uses a related idea in discussing God. If God knows a changing world perfectly and responds to it, then God is not unaffected in every respect. Hartshorne therefore distinguishes necessary divine existence from contingent divine knowledge of particular events.
summaries.summary: Charles Hartshorne developed a theocentric metaphysics influenced by process thought, pragmatism, Plato, and Charles Sanders Peirce. He defended philosophical theism and helped renew interest in Anselm’s ontological argument, but his main contribution concerned God’s actuality: the manner in which God exists. Classical theism commonly treats God as necessary, timeless, immutable, and omnipotent. Hartshorne’s neoclassical theism is dipolar. It attributes to God the highest forms of permanence and change, unity and plurality, activity and receptivity. God exists necessarily, but God’s knowledge of contingent events and responses to creatures are not fixed in advance. Because the future contains genuine possibilities, divine omniscience means knowing the past as actual, the present as far as it is knowable, and future possibilities as possibilities. Hartshorne therefore replaces absolute omnipotence with ideal power: God has the greatest power possible in a world containing other partially free agents. He interprets God as panentheistically related to the world, sometimes using the analogy of a mind or soul to a body. His ontological argument holds that existence by itself may not be a predicate, but necessary or contingent existence is philosophically significant. He claims that a possible perfect being cannot be merely contingent, so the central task is to show that God is not impossible. Hartshorne’s psychicalism extends minimal experience to all concrete dynamic individuals, while denying that abstractions and mere aggregates, such as a table or flock, experience as wholes. key_ideas: Hartshorne’s method combines exhaustive comparison of alternatives, historical study, and moderation between extremes; it is not simply rationalism.
His version of the ontological argument distinguishes necessary, contingent, and impossible existence, arguing that a possible greatest being cannot exist merely contingently.
He separates God’s necessary existence from God’s changing knowledge and response to a partly indeterminate future.
Against classical omnipotence, he argues for ideal power limited by the real powers and partial freedom of creatures.
Psychicalism is meant to avoid both mind-body dualism and materialism by treating experience as present in graduated forms throughout nature.
His account of value supports environmental concern and rejects anthropocentrism, while his contributionism denies personal immortality but says lives can remain present in divine memory.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hartshorne’s philosophy links questions often kept apart: the logic of God’s existence, the reality of time, freedom, suffering, consciousness, and the value of nonhuman nature. Its importance lies partly in showing how a different account of divine perfection changes theology and ethics. The entry also presents serious criticism, especially the challenge that Hartshorne may draw the contrast between classical and neoclassical theism too sharply. Studying that disagreement helps clarify how philosophical systems depend on connected assumptions.

important_terms.definition: The study of the most general features of reality, including existence, time, possibility, mind, and God.
The position that all concrete, active individuals possess some minimal form of experience or feeling, without necessarily having consciousness or thought.
A philosophical view that treats becoming, events, and relations as fundamental features of reality.
The claim that God exists necessarily: God could not fail to exist if God is possible.
The distinction between what must be the case and what may or may not be the case.
The view that the world is included in God, while God remains distinguishable from the world.
A theory of value concerned with goodness, beauty, and what is worth pursuing or protecting.
A two-sided account of perfection that values the best forms of both stability and change, rather than treating one side as wholly divine and the other as defective.

questions_to_think_about: Does necessary existence describe a real feature of a being, or only how we use words?
Can God know every future possibility without knowing the future as already fixed?
Does the existence of suffering count against omnipotence, or only against a particular definition of omnipotence?
Is psychicalism a genuine explanation of experience, or an overly broad use of the word feeling?
Can classical and neoclassical accounts of God be combined, as William Alston suggests?

summaries.example: Think about a group project. The past choices of the group affect what can happen next, but they do not decide every detail. A good team leader cannot control every person, yet can understand the group, respond to problems, and help it do its best. Hartshorne uses a similar picture for God: the world has real powers and some freedom, while God has the greatest possible power and responds to what happens.
summaries.summary: Charles Hartshorne was a major philosopher of religion and metaphysics who defended the rationality of theism. He was also known for process-based thinking, in which change and relationships are central. Hartshorne agreed with traditional thinkers that God is supreme, but he disagreed about what divine perfection requires. Classical theism often describes God as outside time, completely unchanging, and able to do anything logically possible. Hartshorne’s neoclassical view says that God exists necessarily but lives through time, continually responds to the world, and is perfected through an everlasting process. God knows everything that can be known: the past as settled, the present as limited by physical conditions, and the future as a range of possibilities and probabilities. Hartshorne calls this ideal power rather than absolute omnipotence, because creatures have some real power of their own. He also uses panentheism to describe a God who includes the world while remaining distinct from it. In his reasoning about God’s existence, Hartshorne separates three possibilities: God is impossible, God exists only contingently, or God exists necessarily. He argues that a greatest conceivable being could not be merely contingent. Hartshorne’s other major idea is psychicalism. He rejects both mind-body dualism, which treats mind and matter as separate kinds of reality, and materialism, which explains reality only in physical terms. He argues that concrete individuals, including very small natural units, have minimal experience, though they are not necessarily conscious or intelligent. key_ideas: Hartshorne studied every major option he could find, looked at earlier philosophers, and then tried to avoid extreme positions.
He defended a version of the ontological argument by saying that a perfect being, if possible, would have to exist necessarily rather than only possibly.
He believed God exists necessarily but changes through time by responding to creatures and their partly open future.
He rejected unlimited omnipotence in favor of power that is as great as possible while other beings retain some power and freedom.
His psychicalism says that experience comes in degrees, from simple activity in nature to complex human awareness.
He argued that nonhuman nature has value beyond its usefulness to people and connected philosophy with environmental ethics.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hartshorne matters because he offers a connected way to think about religion, science, time, freedom, suffering, and environmental responsibility. His account is not accepted by everyone. Critics have questioned whether his picture of God is compatible with traditional theism and whether experience can meaningfully be attributed to very small natural units. Those disagreements make his work useful for learning how philosophical arguments are built and challenged.

important_terms.definition: The study of reality at its most general level, including questions about existence, change, mind, and God.
The belief that every concrete, active part of nature has some very basic kind of feeling or experience.
Hartshorne’s preferred name for panpsychism, emphasizing that the view concerns experience rather than full human-like minds.
The view that change, events, and relationships are basic features of reality.
The difference between what must exist, what might exist, and what cannot exist.
The idea that all things are in God, but God is not simply identical with all things.
The study of value, including goodness, beauty, and what deserves care.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a philosopher prefer a middle position between total determinism and total randomness?
What is the difference between God existing necessarily and God knowing a particular event contingently?
Would a God who can control everything leave room for creaturely freedom?
Does saying that cells have simple experience differ from saying that they have thoughts?
Should nature be protected because it is useful, because it is beautiful, or because it has value in itself?
